power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p ≤ 0.002", "p ≤ 5.3 × 10 -16", 
"p ≤ 2.7 × 10 -5"), Text = c("In ADNI3, the model retained a mean Dice of 0.70 (SD 0.14) without retraining and exceeded all comparators (FDR-adjusted p ≤ 0.002).", 
"Mean Dice was 0.50 for SHIVA-WMH, 0.57 for segcsvdWMH, and 0.29 for WMH-SynthSeg (Friedman p < 0.001; FDR-adjusted Wilcoxon p ≤ 5.3 × 10 -16 for each comparison with the proposed model; Table 2).", 
"Across cohorts, mean Dice for the proposed model was 0.73 in ADNI 2D, 0.76 in WWISH 2D, 0.74 in WWISH 3D, and 0.67 in UKB 3D, and it exceeded each comparator in every cohort-byacquisition stratum (FDR-adjusted p ≤ 2.7 × 10 -5 ; Table 2; Supplementary Figure S2)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

text.text: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are increasingly pooled across aging, cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD), and dementia cohorts that differ in both disease composition and FLAIR acquisition.

Most automated segmentation tools were developed within a narrower range of populations or protocols, and few have been tested for whether segmentation accuracy and error remain consistent across conventional 2D and isotropic 3D FLAIR, or whether the choice of algorithm alters downstream clinical associations.

text.text: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are among the most common neuroimaging findings in older adults and are associated with cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD), cognitive decline, stroke, and dementia.

Although WMH are often interpreted as markers of vascular brain injury, their biological substrates are heterogeneous and may reflect contributions from small vessel injury, neurodegeneration, and other vascular and metabolic processes (Wardlaw et al., 2015; Smith and Beaudin, 2018; Vemuri et al., 2022; Maillard et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Although WMH are often interpreted as markers of vascular brain injury, their biological substrates are heterogeneous and may reflect contributions from small vessel injury, neurodegeneration, and other vascular and metabolic processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Wardlaw et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Smith and Beaudin, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Vemuri et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Maillard et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, WMH are increasingly quantified as a continuous marker of cumulative white matter injury across population-based aging studies, vascular cohorts, and studies of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (AD/ADRD) (Garnier-Crussard et al., 2023; DeCarli et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Accordingly, WMH are increasingly quantified as a continuous marker of cumulative white matter injury across population-based aging studies, vascular cohorts, and studies of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (AD/ADRD) <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Garnier-Crussard et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">DeCarli et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Reliable automated segmentation is essential for these applications because manual delineation is labor-intensive, subject to inter-rater variability, and impractical for large, multisite imaging datasets.

The broader use of WMH as a cross-disease imaging biomarker, however, presents a substantial translational challenge because models are often applied to populations that differ from their development cohorts in both clinical characteristics and MRI acquisition protocols.

Contemporary neuroimaging studies frequently combine participants with different disease profiles and lesion burdens whose scans were acquired on different scanners and with different FLAIR protocols, including conventional thick-slice 2D and approximately isotropic 3D sequences.

Segmentation performance can vary across these conditions, particularly in participants with low WMH burden or small punctate lesions, and protocol-dependent errors may introduce systematic differences in estimated WMH volume (Heinen et al., 2019; Hotz et al., 2022; Kuijf et al., 2019; Tubi et al., 2020; Torres-Simon et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Segmentation performance can vary across these conditions, particularly in participants with low WMH burden or small punctate lesions, and protocol-dependent errors may introduce systematic differences in estimated WMH volume <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Heinen et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Hotz et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Kuijf et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Tubi et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Torres-Simon et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Methods developed within a particular disease spectrum or acquisition setting may therefore perform less consistently when both the population and imaging protocol differ from their development distributions (Caligiuri et al., 2015; Balakrishnan et al., 2021; Rahmani et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Methods developed within a particular disease spectrum or acquisition setting may therefore perform less consistently when both the population and imaging protocol differ from their development distributions <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Caligiuri et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Balakrishnan et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Rahmani et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This mismatch complicates pooled analyses and may force investigators to use different algorithms across sub-cohorts, exclude incompatible acquisitions, or deploy a single method beyond the setting in which it was validated.
Recent deep-learning methods have substantially advanced automated WMH segmentation.

SHIVA-WMH has demonstrated sensitivity to early WMH in vascular and aging cohorts, segcsvdWMH was developed using heterogeneous datasets to quantify WMH in CSVD and related clinical populations, and WMH-SynthSeg was designed to support segmentation across heterogeneous clinical MRI data (Gibson et al., 2024; Laso et al., 2024; Tsuchida et al., 2024).
text.formatted: SHIVA-WMH has demonstrated sensitivity to early WMH in vascular and aging cohorts, segcsvdWMH was developed using heterogeneous datasets to quantify WMH in CSVD and related clinical populations, and WMH-SynthSeg was designed to support segmentation across heterogeneous clinical MRI data <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Gibson et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Laso et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Tsuchida et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These methods address important dimensions of population or acquisition heterogeneity.

However, evidence remains limited for a single empirically trained model designed and evaluated across the intersection of neurodegenerative, vascular, and population-based cohorts and both conventional 2D and isotropic 3D FLAIR acquisitions.

Moreover, relatively few studies have determined whether performance is maintained across lesion burden and lesion size, tested transfer to an unseen acquisition configuration, or examined whether algorithm-dependent differences in WMH quantification alter downstream clinical information (Tubi et al., 2020; Gesierich et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Moreover, relatively few studies have determined whether performance is maintained across lesion burden and lesion size, tested transfer to an unseen acquisition configuration, or examined whether algorithm-dependent differences in WMH quantification alter downstream clinical information <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Tubi et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Gesierich et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Addressing this intersectional gap is necessary to establish a consistent WMH measure for large, heterogeneous neuroimaging studies.

In this study, we used the self-configuring nnU-Net framework (Isensee et al., 2021) to develop a single WMH segmentation model using three complementary cohorts: the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), representing the neurodegenerative disease spectrum; the Washington University White Matter Ischemic-Hypoxia study (WWISH), enriched for CSVD and contributing paired 2D and 3D FLAIR acquisitions; and UK Biobank (UKB), representing population-based aging.
text.formatted: In this study, we used the self-configuring nnU-Net framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Isensee et al., 2021)</ref> to develop a single WMH segmentation model using three complementary cohorts: the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), representing the neurodegenerative disease spectrum; the Washington University White Matter Ischemic-Hypoxia study (WWISH), enriched for CSVD and contributing paired 2D and 3D FLAIR acquisitions; and UK Biobank (UKB), representing population-based aging.

text.text: Together, these cohorts encompass substantial variation in WMH burden, lesion morphology, disease context, and FLAIR acquisitions.

We addressed four questions: 1) whether the model provides accurate and consistent overall segmentation across cohorts and acquisition types relative to contemporary benchmark methods; 2) whether it maintains sensitivity to small lesions and low WMH burden; 3) whether the model maintains its performance on an independent set of ADNI 3D FLAIR scans not used for model development or tuning; and 4) whether its WMH volume estimates provide incremental information about incident dementia beyond established clinical predictors.

We hypothesized that deliberately incorporating heterogeneity in disease context, lesion burden, and acquisition into model development would produce a single deployable model with consistent segmentation performance across the evaluated imaging settings and clinically informative WMH estimates.
We assembled a multi-cohort imaging dataset designed to reflect the heterogeneity of populations and FLAIR acquisitions encountered in aging and cerebrovascular research.

Participants were drawn from three cohorts: the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), representing an AD-focused neurodegenerative cohort; the Washington University White Matter Ischemic-Hypoxia study (WWISH), representing a CSVD-enriched cohort; and the UK Biobank (UKB), representing population-based aging.
Together, these cohorts encompassed a broad range of WMH burden, lesion morphology, clinical context, and 2D and 3D FLAIR acquisition protocols.
The model-development dataset comprised 460 FLAIR scans from 330 unique participants.
ADNI contributed one 2D FLAIR scan from each of 100 participants spanning cognitively unimpaired, mild cognitive impairment, and dementia groups.
WWISH contributed same-visit paired 2D and 3D FLAIR scans from 130 participants with clinically defined CSVD, for a total of 260 scans.
UKB contributed one 3D FLAIR scan from each of 100 community-dwelling participants, generally characterized by lower WMH burden.
The dataset was partitioned using participant-level grouping, such that each participant was assigned exclusively to the training, validation, or internal test set.
For WWISH participants, paired 2D and 3D FLAIR scans were assigned together to the same partition, preventing subjectlevel information leakage across partitions.

The internal held-out test set comprised 92 scans from 66 unique participants: 20 ADNI participants with one 2D FLAIR scan each, 26 WWISH participants with paired 2D and 3D FLAIR scans, and 20 UKB participants with one 3D FLAIR scan each.
The remaining 368 scans from 264 participants formed the model-development set used for training and validation.

Within the development set, participant-level grouping was maintained throughout model fitting and validation so that both WWISH acquisitions from a given participant remained in the same subset (training or validation).
External validation was performed in an independent ADNI3 test cohort of 25 nonoverlapping participants with 3D FLAIR imaging that was entirely withheld from model development and tuning.

text.text: The network received two input channels: the preprocessed FLAIR image and the coregistered T1weighted image. nnU-Net automatically configures network architecture, patch size, batch size, and other training parameters according to the properties of the input dataset.
The resulting model used an encoder-decoder architecture with skip connections, instance normalization, and leaky rectified linear unit activations.
Both native 2D and native 3D FLAIR acquisitions were represented as 3D image volumes after preprocessing and resampling, and coregistration to the T1-weighted image.
The same network was therefore applied to both acquisition types; separate 2D-and 3D-specific networks were not trained.
This design was intended to produce a single model deployable across the range of FLAIR protocols represented in the development data.

A central feature of the training strategy was the deliberate integration of three complementary cohorts spanning neurodegenerative disease, CSVD, and population-based aging, together with both 2D and 3D FLAIR acquisitions.

This design exposed a single model to variation in clinical context, WMH burden and morphology, and FLAIR acquisition during training, rather than developing separate disease-or sequence-specific models.
Training patches were sampled from the preprocessed FLAIR and T1-weighted images and corresponding reference masks and underwent the standard nnU-Net on-the-fly spatial and intensity augmentations.
The model was optimized using a composite Dice and cross-entropy loss to address the substantial class imbalance between WMH and non-WMH voxels.

text.text: We developed a single nnU-Net WMH segmentation model trained across neurodegenerative, CSVD-enriched, and population-based cohorts and across conventional 2D and isotropic 3D FLAIR.
Four findings support its use as a common segmentation approach in multi-cohort studies.
First, the model outperformed three contemporary tools at the voxel, volume, and lesion levels in a held-out internal test set.
Second, accuracy was similar on 2D and 3D FLAIR, and volume bias relative to acquisition-specific references varied less between paired acquisitions than comparator biases.
Third, its advantage was largest where WMH measurement is most difficult: in low-burden scans and for small lesions.
Fourth, performance transferred to an unseen ADNI3 3D FLAIR protocol, and model-derived volumes added information about incident dementia beyond clinical covariates.

The principal contribution is therefore not the nnU-Net architecture itself, but the development and validation of a single model across heterogeneous disease contexts and acquisitions, together with evidence that algorithm-dependent differences in WMH quantification can affect downstream clinical inference.
Acquisition-related segmentation bias is an important consideration in multi-cohort studies.
Differences in error between 2D and 3D FLAIR can complicate comparisons when acquisition type varies by cohort, site, or study phase.
The same-visit paired WWISH scans allowed us to assess these differences within participants.

The proposed model's mean volume bias relative to acquisition-specific references differed by less than 2 mL between acquisitions, compared with approximately 5-10 mL for the comparators; SHIVA-WMH also showed reversals in bias direction.
These findings are consistent with Hotz et al. (2022), who reported different algorithm biases on 2D and 3D FLAIR relative to acquisition-specific manual references.
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Hotz et al. (2022)</ref>, who reported different algorithm biases on 2D and 3D FLAIR relative to acquisition-specific manual references.

text.text: Expert reference volumes themselves were, on average, 6.3 mL larger on 2D than on 3D FLAIR, and the proposed model's volumes differed in the same direction.
Thus, similar accuracy against acquisitionspecific references does not establish interchangeability of 2D-and 3D-derived volumes.
The largest gains were in low-burden scans and small lesions, where existing tools differed most from the reference.
This range matters because many population-based and preclinical samples, such as UKB, have total WMH volumes below 5 mL, where measurement error is large relative to between-person variation.

The proposed model's higher sensitivity did not come at the cost of more false-positive lesions than SHIVA-WMH, and the low false-positive count of segcsvdWMH reflected conservative segmentation that missed many small lesions.

SHIVA-WMH, which was developed with isotropic 3D FLAIR to detect punctate lesions (Tsuchida et al., 2024), matched the proposed model's very-small-lesion overlap on 3D FLAIR but not on 2D FLAIR, consistent with the importance of training-data acquisition for small-lesion detection.

text.text: More reliable detection at low burden may increase the usefulness of WMH as an early marker in cognitively unimpaired and population samples, although this requires direct testing in longitudinal data.

These comparisons should be interpreted in light of each comparator's design. segcsvdWMH was trained on heterogeneous 2D and 3D FLAIR from CSVD-related clinical cohorts (Gibson et al., 2024); SHIVA-WMH was trained on isotropic 3D FLAIR from young adults combined with the MICCAI WMH Segmentation Challenge data (Tsuchida et al., 2024); and WMH-SynthSeg was designed to be contrast-and resolution-agnostic across clinical and low-field MRI rather than to maximize accuracy on research-grade FLAIR (Laso et al., 2024).

text.text: Input requirements also differed: our proposed model and SHIVA-WMH used both FLAIR and T1-weighted images, whereas segcsvdWMH and WMH-SynthSeg were run using FLAIR images alone.
Comparator Dice values in our data were lower than those reported in their development studies.
This likely reflects, in part, differences between our reference labeling convention and theirs, in addition to differences in populations and protocols.
Because the proposed model was trained on masks generated with the same convention used for evaluation, voxel-level benchmarking alone may favor it.
The incident dementia analysis does not depend on reference masks and therefore provides a complementary, label-independent comparison.
The proposed model also exceeded segcsvdWMH within WWISH on both 2D and 3D FLAIR, although the margin was smaller on 3D (0.74 vs.
0.66), and segcsvdWMH was the closest competitor in ADNI3, with similar volumetric error to the proposed model.
Algorithm choice also influenced downstream clinical inference.

All four methods were applied to the same participants and evaluated using the same clinical covariates, yet only WMH volume from the proposed model significantly improved model fit for incident dementia.
Volumes from SHIVA-WMH and WMH-SynthSeg showed weaker associations, and segcsvdWMH-derived volume showed no association.
These results extend prior evidence that WMH-cognition associations depend on the segmentation algorithm (Tubi et al., 2020).

text.text: However, absolute AUC gains were modest.
These findings provide complementary evidence of the clinical relevance of the proposed model's WMH estimates; they do not establish a validated clinical prediction tool.
Its stronger performance in low-burden scans and small lesions may contribute to the observed associations, although this explanation requires direct testing.
The dementia analysis combined 2D and 3D FLAIR scans from ADNI and Knight ADRC; additional adjustment for acquisition type did not change the association for the proposed model.
For multi-cohort studies, these results support applying a single segmentation model across the evaluated disease contexts and acquisitions, reducing the need to switch algorithms between cohorts.
This removes algorithm choice as one source of methodological variation, but does not eliminate acquisition-related differences in WMH volume.

Acquisition type should therefore remain part of the analytical design, and comparable segmentation accuracy should not be taken to imply that unadjusted 2D-and 3D-derived volumes can be pooled interchangeably.
Future work could evaluate whether incorporating paired acquisitions during training improves crossacquisition volume consistency while preserving segmentation accuracy.

This study has several strengths, including deliberately heterogeneous training data, same-visit paired 2D and 3D acquisitions, head-to-head benchmarking at the voxel, volume, and lesion levels, evaluation in an unseen acquisition protocol, and a label-independent clinical validation.
Several limitations warrant consideration.
First, although the cohorts were diverse, they do not capture the full range of scanners, field strengths, acquisition protocols, and populations encountered in practice.
Second, reference masks were initialized using an automated method and refined by a single rater with neurologist adjudication.

Inter-rater Dice agreement, previously assessed in a subset, was 0.72 (95% CI, 0.67-0.81; Phuah et al., 2022), comparable to the model's mean Dice in the internal test set (0.73), suggesting that model-reference agreement approached the level of agreement between human raters.

text.text: However, reliability was not reassessed here, and systematic labeling conventions may be shared by training and evaluation.

Third, the external ADNI3 test set included distinct participants and acquisition protocol but originated from the same consortium as part of the development data, and its size was modest (n = 25), although comparable to or larger than the labeled external test sets used to validate SHIVA-WMH (n = 11) and segcsvdWMH (n = 10); fully independent validation in larger cohorts remains necessary.

Fourth, paired WWISH acquisitions contributed correlated observations to pooled analyses, although results were consistent in acquisition-specific strata in which each participant contributed one scan.

Fifth, reference masks were defined separately for each acquisition, allowing assessment of segmentation accuracy but not determination of which acquisition more accurately measured the underlying lesion burden.
Direct cross-acquisition agreement was also assessed in only 26 participants from a single cohort.
Sixth, the model requires both FLAIR and a coregistered T1-weighted image, which may limit its use in datasets without T1-weighted imaging or with poor FLAIR-T1 registration.
It was also evaluated crosssectionally; its accuracy for measuring longitudinal change and its regional performance remain to be established.
Finally, clinical validation was limited to progression on the global CDR in a modest sample.

Pooled and longitudinal WMH studies combine cohorts that differ in disease composition and FLAIR protocol, creating the potential for acquisition-related measurement differences to be mistaken for biological differences between cohorts, sites, or study phases.
Our findings show that algorithm choice matters: segmentation methods differed in acquisition-dependent bias and in the clinical information their WMH estimates provided.

A single model trained across disease contexts and both 2D and 3D FLAIR achieved similar segmentation accuracy on both acquisitions and more stable volume bias relative to acquisition-specific references than the comparator tools.
These results support using a common segmentation approach across heterogeneous cohorts, reducing the need to exclude scans or switch algorithms solely because of acquisition type.
Public release of the model will facilitate its use in multi-cohort aging, vascular, and neurodegenerative studies, including studies that span protocol transitions.
